newsitem.title: CHINA: China envoy Zhou bows out of Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China envoy Zhou bows out of Hong Kong.

text.p: China staged a gala ceremony on Monday to announce the departure of Zhou Nan, its top envoy in Hong Kong who waged endless battles with former British governor Chris Patten in the last years of colonial rule.

Zhou, 69, had flown in from Beijing on Saturday to hand over formally to Jiang Enzhu the directorship of the Xinhua News Agency branch in Hong Kong, which until the July 1 handover of sovereignty had acted as Beijing's main voice in Hong Kong.

Looking haggard, Zhou, who had undergone an operation in Beijing in July to remove a stomach tumour, was wheeled out of his plane on Saturday and in the large ballroom where China hosted his farewell reception, two aides helped him on stage.
The hardliner, who acted as an interrogator of American prisoners during the Korean War, helped steer Hong Kong back to China at midnight June 30, ending 156 years of British rule.
The Xinhua office, which Zhou headed since February 1990, had been China's de facto mission in the territory until the handover, and is known to represent China's Communist Party.
It also acted as a watchdog and shadow government in the colonial era and its deputy directors were like shadow ministers, tracking specific policy areas.
Now a Special Administrative Region (SAR) in China, Hong Kong is promised a high degree of autonomy under a "one country, two systems" formula, except in defence and foreign affairs.
Zhou, who sat on stage with top China representatives in the territory and Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa, issued a note of confidence before more than 1,500 guests.

"Now, 'one country, two systems' has already been successfully implemented in Hong Kong and turned from a great concept into living reality," Zhou said before a power-packed audience comprising prominent businessmen, foreign diplomats, local politicians and lawmakers.
His successor Jiang, an expert on Hong Kong matters and who until early this year was China's ambassador to Britain, said Xinhua would not interfere in the internal affairs of Hong Kong.

"With the return of Hong Kong to her motherland, its functions will be appropriately adjusted as necessary, but it will not interfere in the affairs which fall in the domain of the high degree of autonomy of the Hong Kong SAR," Jiang said.
Breaking away from the stern and unapproachable image of his predecessor, Jiang later came before the large media corps after he saw off Zhou, who was wheeled out of the ballroom.
"Xinhua's foreign affairs role in Hong Kong has already been handed over to (China's) Foreign Ministry office," Jiang said.
